candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 24 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 25 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 26 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 27 not required. 28
candidates.context: The purpose of this guidance is to provide recommendations to sponsors regarding clinical trial 16 designs for drugs and biologics 2 intended for the treatment of adults with endogenous Cushing’s 17 syndrome for whom surgery is not an option or has not been curative. This guidance does not 18 address development of drugs and biologics for the treatment of exogenous Cushing’s syndrome. 19 This guidance is intended to focus continued discussions among FDA’s Division of General 20 Endocrinology, pharmaceutical sponsors, the academic community, and the public. 3 This is the 21 first guidance drafted by FDA on this topic. 22

candidates.context: The following are the overall objectives of a clinical development program for a drug intended 74 for the treatment of Cushing’s syndrome: determine the pharmacokinetics and 75 pharmacodynamics of the drug in subjects with Cushing’s syndrome, evaluate the dose (and/or 76 exposure)-response relationship to support dose selection for phase 3 pivotal studies, and 77 establish the efficacy and safety of the drug in subjects with Cushing’s syndrome. 78 Other clinical pharmacology studies, including assessment of drug interactions 9 and the impact 89 of intrinsic and other extrinsic factors on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the 90 investigational drug, should be conducted early in drug development to aid in the trial design of 91 later phase trials. 92

candidates.statement: 10 See FD&C Act section 505(d) (21 U.S.C. 355(d)). For a drug product to be approved by FDA, a sponsor must provide substantial evidence that the drug has the effect it purports to have under the conditions of use described in the proposed labeling and that the drug’s benefits outweigh the risks. Generally, the evidence is derived from adequate and well-controlled clinical studies.

candidates.statement: The proposed indication for the drug should reflect the disease subtypes and endpoints studied in 115 the pivotal phase 3 trials. Because some subtypes of Cushing’s syndrome are rare (e.g., ectopic 116 ACTH syndrome, adrenal carcinoma, pituitary carcinoma) and it may be challenging to enroll an 117 adequate number of subjects with those subtypes in a clinical trial, FDA will review all available 118 data obtained in even a limited number of subjects. FDA may also consider how data from a 119 broader Cushing’s syndrome clinical trial population may apply to the treatment of rarer 120 subtypes, potentially based on the drug’s mechanism of action. For example, sponsors may 121 provide a rationale that data from clinical trials of steroidogenesis inhibitors in subjects with 122 Cushing’s disease can support approval of the drug for patients with Cushing’s syndrome of 123 other rarer subtypes given that the drug inhibits cortisol synthesis, irrespective of the underlying 124 pathophysiology. 125

candidates.statement: Active-controlled trials should use a U.S.-approved drug as a comparator, dosed according to the 200 recommended dosage in FDA-approved labeling, and titrated, as tolerated, to the maximum 201 recommended approved dosage in subjects who do not adequately respond to the lower dosages. 202 If the test drug and comparator have different routes of administration or different regimens, 203 sponsors should consider a double-dummy trial design in order to yield interpretable efficacy and 204 safety data. 205
candidates.context: Placebo-controlled trials have been conducted to support approval of drugs for the indication of 191 both Cushing’s syndrome and Cushing’s disease. Although some stakeholders have raised 192 concerns about the ethics of a placebo control, this design is regarded as acceptable because 193 monitoring and timely control of Cushing’s syndrome–related comorbidities during the trial 194 (e.g., with antidiabetic drugs and antihypertensive drugs) and other protocol safeguards (e.g., 195 inclusion and exclusion criteria, withdrawal criteria) can ensure the safety of subjects. Limitation 196 of the trial duration in a placebo-controlled trial can minimize other disease-related impacts, 197 including osteoporosis, infection, and muscle loss. 198 5. Efficacy Endpoints 207

candidates.statement: The choice of efficacy endpoints should reflect the drug’s mechanism of action. UFC is a reliable 209 marker to assess the efficacy of drugs that inhibit either pituitary ACTH secretion or adrenal 210 steroidogenesis. In contrast, UFC is not a reliable biomarker for drugs that block cortisol 211 receptors. Efficacy for this class of drugs should be established by assessing their impact on 212 downstream effects of cortisol at the glucocorticoid receptor. 213

candidates.statement: The primary efficacy analysis should be a responder analysis, in which a responder is a subject 225 with elevated UFC levels at baseline who achieved normal UFC levels at the end of the trial. 226 Absolute change in UFC levels from baseline to end of treatment is not a meaningful endpoint 227 because there is lack of consensus on what constitutes an important change from baseline in UFC 228 levels. Rather, per treatment guidelines, normalization of UFC is indicative of disease control. 229 Because UFC levels can fluctuate in patients with Cushing’s syndrome, mean UFC levels from a 230 minimum of two adequate urinary collections at both baseline and endpoint should be used for 231 the primary efficacy analysis. Subjects who required a dose increase during the fixed-dose 232
candidates.context: FDA accepts as a primary efficacy endpoint the sustained normalization of mean UFC levels 217 (i.e., UFC ≤ULN ) after a titration phase followed by a fixed-dose period of adequate duration. 218 Treatment guidelines 13 recommend normalization of UFC as the goal of therapy because 219 normalization is associated with reduced morbidity and mortality. Furthermore, UFC is an 220 objective endpoint and is supported by clear mechanistic rationale. All currently marketed drugs 221 that decrease cortisol levels in patients with Cushing’s syndrome were approved based on the 222 biochemical control of the disease, (i.e., normalization of UFC levels). 223 13 See the Treatment of Cushing’s Syndrome Guideline Resources web page, available at https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/treatment-of-cushing-syndrome#1 .

candidates.statement: Change in mean systolic blood pressure (SBP) and/or diastolic blood pressure (DBP) from 281 baseline to the end of the treatment period based on ambulatory blood pressure monitoring is an 282 objective laboratory measure to demonstrate an effect of diminished cortisol action in subjects 283 with glucocorticoid-induced hypertension. candidates.statement: • Trial protocols and statistical analysis plans should clearly prespecify the estimands of 459 primary interest. The description of the estimands should reflect the clinical questions of 460 interest in respect to thoughtfully envisioned intercurrent events. 17 The statistical 461 analyses should be aligned with the estimands of primary interest and clearly specify how 462 intercurrent events and missing data will be accounted for. Sponsors should consult with 463 FDA about these issues during the trial design stage. Sponsors should provide adequate 464 justifications that the proposed estimands address meaningful clinical questions of 465 interest and can be estimated with plausible assumptions. Refer to ICH E9(R1) for more 466 discussions on estimands and intercurrent events. 467

candidates.statement: • The imputation of missing data typically relies on some assumptions of missing 501 mechanisms that are not verifiable. To assess the sensitivity of results to such uncertainty, 502 sponsors should conduct sensitivity analyses, such as tipping point analyses, that vary 503 assumptions about the missing data. The tipping point analyses should allow assumptions 504 about the missing outcomes on the two treatment arms to vary independently and should 505 also include scenarios where missing data on one treatment arm indicates worse 506 outcomes than missing data on the other treatment arm. The goal is to evaluate the 507 plausibility of the assumed expected values for missing outcomes on each treatment arm 508 under which the conclusions change (i.e., under which there is no longer evidence of a 509 treatment effect). For continuous data, we recommend centering the tipping point 510 analysis around the analysis that most appropriately addresses missing data. 511
